title: Chapter 2 — The Modern Appliance Buyer
intro: Your customer has changed. They have already researched, compared, and formed opinions before they walk through your door. Understanding how they buy — not just what they buy — is the foundation of everything you will learn in this program.

sections.title: The Customer Has Already Started Without You
sections.content:
Here is a number that should change the way you think about every person who walks through your door: 56% of appliance buyers research online before ever entering a store. They have watched YouTube reviews. They have compared prices. They have read owner reviews. They have explored specifications and viewed 3D product renderings.

By the time they are standing in front of you, they are not starting from zero. They are continuing a journey. Your job is to pick up where they left off — not restart the process as if they know nothing.

The salesperson who says 'let me show you what we have' is ignoring everything the customer already did on their own time. The salesperson who says 'what have you found so far that you liked?' is joining their process. That is a fundamentally different conversation.

sections.title: The 8-Stage Buying Cycle
sections.content:
People do not wake up one morning thinking 'I should spend $3,000 on a refrigerator.' The decision to buy a major appliance follows a predictable path. Understanding that path tells you where the customer is and what they need from you right now.

Stage 1 — Trigger Event (3 to 24 months before purchase): Something starts the process. A kitchen renovation. A new home. An appliance aging. A breakdown. Education begins.

Stage 2 — Passive Research (2 to 12 months before): Browsing Pinterest, YouTube, retailer websites. They are gathering ideas, not making decisions.

Stage 3 — Active Research (2 to 8 weeks before): Comparing brands, reading reviews, measuring space. They are narrowing options.

Stage 4 — Store Visits (1 to 4 weeks before): Touching products, asking questions. This is where you become critical.

Stage 5 — Decision (same day to 2 weeks): Comparing financing, promotions, delivery options. They are ready but need confidence.

Stage 6 — Purchase (day zero): Order placed.

Stage 7 — Delivery and Installation (2 days to 8 weeks): Excitement mixed with anxiety. Communication matters.

Stage 8 — Ownership (5 to 20 years): Daily use. Reviews. Referrals. Future purchases.

Most salespeople only engage at Stage 4. The best salespeople understand all eight stages and meet the customer wherever they are.

sections.title: How Long Does It Actually Take?
sections.content:
The average buying cycle depends heavily on what they are buying.

Microwave: same day to 3 days. Dishwasher: 1 to 3 weeks. Range: 2 to 4 weeks. Refrigerator: 2 to 8 weeks. Laundry pair: 1 to 4 weeks. Built-in appliances: 2 to 6 months. Full kitchen package: 3 to 12 months. Luxury kitchen over $20,000: 6 to 18 months.

The weighted average across all purchase types — excluding emergency replacements — is about 35 days from the moment someone becomes an active buyer until they purchase. That breaks down to roughly 14 days of research, 10 days of store visits and comparisons, and 11 days of decision-making.

Why does this matter? Because a customer buying a microwave today needs a completely different conversation than someone planning a kitchen renovation over six months. The 10 Steps of Selling apply to both — but the pace, the depth, and the follow-up look completely different.

sections.title: What Stops People from Buying
sections.content:
This is where it gets interesting — and where most salespeople miss the real problem.

33% of customers leave because they cannot find the features they want. Not the price. The features. That tells you something important: if you do not complete a thorough discovery and understand exactly what they are looking for, a third of your customers may walk out because they never found what they came in for — even though you probably had it.

20% do not buy because the desired model is out of stock. That is an inventory problem, not a sales problem. But a great salesperson can navigate it.

Price remains the number-one purchase driver — but here is the thing most people miss: only 21% of shoppers even negotiate. Of those who do negotiate, roughly 66% receive a discount with a median savings of about $123. That means 79% of your customers are not pushing back on price at all. If you are losing sales and blaming price, you are probably wrong about why.

sections.title: The Customer You Never See Coming
sections.content:
75% of appliance buyers purchase on their first store visit once they have decided to shop. Read that again. Three out of four customers are ready to buy the day they walk in.

But 71% still complete the purchase in a physical store — not online. Even in 2026, the physical showroom matters. Customers want to touch the product, see it in person, ask questions, and feel confident.

29% complete the entire purchase online. That number is growing. If your store is not set up to sell through live chat, video calls, or online — you are ignoring nearly a third of buyers. Every channel is a showroom.

32% visit the manufacturer's website during their journey, but only 1.6% buy directly from the manufacturer. The manufacturer is educating them. You are selling to them. Understand the difference.

sections.title: Why They Choose You — Or Someone Else
sections.content:
When you ask what actually causes someone to buy from a particular store, the answers are revealing.

Salesperson recommendation: 31%. This is the single biggest factor. You — the person standing on the floor — influence nearly a third of all purchase decisions. That should tell you how important your process is.

Online reviews: 22%. What other customers said about their experience matters almost as much as what you say.

Promotion: 18%. Important but not dominant.

Family recommendation: 14%. Word of mouth is still powerful.

Brand loyalty: 9%. Smaller than most people think.

Display in store: 6%. The showroom matters, but less than the person in it.

The takeaway is clear: you are the competitive advantage. Not the price. Not the brand. Not the promotion. The salesperson who runs a better process wins more sales. That is what the 10 Steps are built to do.

sections.title: Value Creates Loyalty — Discounts Create Bargain Hunters
sections.content:
Here is a statistic that should shape how you sell every day.

Customers who bought because of price alone: 38% would definitely buy the same brand again.

Customers who bought because of energy efficiency: 56% would definitely buy the same brand again.

Customers who bought because of warranty or guarantee: significantly higher satisfaction than price-driven buyers.

Selling value creates repeat customers. Selling discounts creates bargain hunters who will leave you the moment someone offers a lower price.

This does not mean price does not matter. It means price should not be the only reason someone buys from you. When you build value through great discovery, thoughtful recommendations, and a professional experience — the customer comes back. When you just match a competitor's price, they come back only if you match it again next time.

sections.title: The Replacement Cycle — Your Future Business
sections.content:
Every appliance has a lifespan. Understanding that lifespan tells you when your customer will be back.

Refrigerator: 10 to 15 years. Dishwasher: 8 to 12 years. Range: 13 to 18 years. Cooktop and wall oven: 15 to 20 years. Washer: 8 to 12 years. Dryer: 10 to 13 years. Freezer: 12 to 18 years. Range hood: 15 to 20 years.

If you sold someone a washer and dryer today, they will need a new set in roughly 8 to 12 years. If you stay connected — through follow-up, relationship selling, and CRM — that customer comes back to you instead of starting a new Google search. Your CRM is not a database. It is your future income.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating how well a salesperson understands the modern buyer, ask:

Do they recognize where the customer is in the buying cycle before launching into a presentation?
Do they ask what research the customer has already done?
Do they adapt their approach based on whether this is a same-day emergency or a six-month renovation project?
Do they treat online and chat customers with the same process as showroom customers?
Do they follow up with customers who are not ready to buy today — or just wait for the next person to walk through the door?

The modern buyer rewards salespeople who understand their journey. They punish salespeople who ignore it.
